title: How To Respond After An Apathetic, Inattentive Lesson ve-lesson/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses what to do after a lesson lands flat with a disengaged, bored class, arguing the counterintuitive fix is not more energy or reteaching but raising the level of academic challenge. He explains that student apathy often stems from lessons settling into a comfortable, familiar level of difficulty, and recommends three concrete adjustments: shortening directed teaching and getting students working sooner, tightening time limits to create urgency, and deliberately allowing productive frustration by adding extra steps or complexity. Linsin is careful to distinguish this from punishment, framing it instead as a jolt meant to shock students out of malaise and reveal that they're capable of more than previously assumed. He notes the strategy isn't meant for every lesson but is effective used periodically, and closes with the memorable line to 'tighten the screws, up the ante, turn up the heat.'
points: Student apathy and low urgency during lessons often stem from difficulty settling into a comfortable, familiar level, not from lack of teacher energy.
Rather than reteaching or delivering a motivational speech, the recommended fix is raising the level of academic challenge.
Three concrete tactics: shorten directed teaching to get students working sooner, tighten time limits to build urgency, and allow productive frustration through added complexity.
This approach is explicitly distinguished from punishment — it's meant to shock students out of malaise, not penalize them.
The strategy is meant for occasional use, not every lesson, and can reveal students are capable of significantly more than previously assumed.
quotes: You see, the chief reason students become apathetic is because your lessons have remained at the same level of challenge. In other words, they’ve fallen into a comfortable groove and now all feel about the same.
So the solution, the antidote, is to raise the bar. It's to increase the difficulty by asking more of your students.
Shorten the directed teaching portion of your lesson by at least half, and then quickly shift responsibility to your students.
Allow your students to struggle—because a bit of frustration, along with the prospect of failure, is good. It renews their spirit and awakens their desire to care.
Now, it’s important to point out that increasing the intensity and workload isn’t a punishment. It’s merely a way to shock them out of their malaise.
Just smile and carry on. Tighten the screws, up the ante, turn up the heat. It does a class good.
